{{Short description|Electromagnetic stress}}
{{Electromagnetism|cTopic=Electrodynamics}}

In [[classical electromagnetism]], the '''Maxwell stress tensor''' (named after [[James Clerk Maxwell]]) is the [[Cauchy_stress_tensor|stress tensor]] of an [[electromagnetic field]]. In tensor index notation it is given by:
<math display="block">\sigma_{ij} =
  \varepsilon_0 E_i E_j + \frac{1}{\mu_0}B_i B_j - \left(\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2} E^2 + \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}\right) \delta_{ij} ,
</math>
where <math>\varepsilon_0</math> is the [[electric constant]], <math>\mu_0</math> the [[magnetic constant]], ''E'' the [[electric field]], ''B'' the [[magnetic field]], and <math>\delta_{ij}</math> is the [[Kronecker delta]]. In the [[Gaussian units|Gaussian system]], it is given by:
<math display="block">\sigma_{ij} = \frac{1}{4\pi} \left[E_i E_j + H_i H_j - \frac{1}{2} \left(E^2 + H^2\right) \delta_{ij}\right],</math>
where ''H'' is the [[magnetizing field]].
(<math> E^2 </math> etc is the field magnitude squared, though this is slightly non-standard in tensor notation.)

The elements <math>ij</math> have units of force per unit of area (negative pressure), denoting the force parallel to the <math>i</math>th axis suffered by a surface normal to the <math>j</math>th axis per unit of area. As such the diagonal elements give the [[tension (physics)|tension]] acting on the plane normal to the corresponding axis and the off-diagonal elements represent shear stress in the plane.

Expressed in vector/dyad notation we would have:
<math display="block">
\boldsymbol{\sigma} = \varepsilon_0 \mathbf{E} \otimes \mathbf{E} +  \frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{B} - \left(\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2} E^2  - \frac{1}{2\mu_0}B^2 \right)\mathbb{I}
</math>
in SI units or
<math display="block">
\boldsymbol{\sigma} = \frac{1}{4\pi} \left[ \mathbf{E} \otimes \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{H} \otimes \mathbf{H} - \frac{1}{2} \left(E^2 + H^2\right) \mathbb{I} \right]
</math>
in CGS units where <math>\otimes</math> is the [[dyadic product]], and the last tensor is the unit dyadic:
<math display="block">\mathbb{I} \equiv \begin{pmatrix}
    1 & 0 & 0 \\
    0 & 1 & 0 \\
    0 & 0 & 1
  \end{pmatrix} =
  \mathbf{\hat x} \otimes \mathbf{\hat x} + \mathbf{\hat y} \otimes \mathbf{\hat y} + \mathbf{\hat z} \otimes \mathbf{\hat z}
</math>

In the relativistic formulation of electromagnetism, the nine components of the Maxwell stress tensor appear, negated, as components of the [[electromagnetic stress–energy tensor]], which is the electromagnetic component of the total [[stress–energy tensor]]. The latter describes the density and flux of energy and momentum in spacetime.

The following derivation defines the Maxwell stress tensor by way of introducing it so as to show how electromagnetic body forces arise from electrical and magnetic fields. For an explanation more directly as to how the tensor describes stress (in the absence of body forces) see the web article by J.S.Reid <ref>{{cite web |last1=Reid |first1=J.S. |title=Maxwell Stress Tensor |url=https://homepages.abdn.ac.uk/j.s.reid/pages/Maxwell/Legacy/MaxTensor.html |website=Maxwell's Legacy}}</ref>.

== Derivation ==

As outlined below, the electromagnetic force is written in terms of <math>\mathbf{E}</math> and <math>\mathbf{B}</math>. Using [[vector calculus]] and [[Maxwell's equations]], symmetry is sought for in the terms containing <math>\mathbf{E}</math> and <math>\mathbf{B}</math>, and introducing the Maxwell stress tensor simplifies the result.

The derivation follows Griffiths <ref>{{Cite book| title=Introduction to Electrodynamics| last=Griffiths| first=David J.|date=2008| publisher=Benjamin Cummings Inc.| language=en}}</ref> and applies in the case of a vacuum.

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Maxwell's equations in SI units in ''vacuum'' <br /> (for reference)
|-
 ! Name
 ! Differential form
|-
 | Gauss's law (in vacuum)
 | <math>\boldsymbol{\nabla} \cdot \mathbf{E} = \frac {\rho} {\varepsilon_0}</math>
|-
 | Gauss's law for magnetism
 | <math>\boldsymbol{\nabla} \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0</math>
|-
 | Maxwell–Faraday equation<br />(Faraday's law of induction)
 | <math>\boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \mathbf{E} = -\frac{\partial \mathbf{B}} {\partial t}</math>
|-
 | Ampère's circuital law (in vacuum)<br />(with Maxwell's correction)
 | <math>\boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \mathbf{B} = \mu_0 \mathbf{J} + \mu_0 \varepsilon_0 \frac{\partial \mathbf{E}} {\partial t}\ </math>
|}

{{ordered list

|1= Starting with the [[Lorentz force]] law
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \mathbf{F} &= q(\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}) \\[3pt]
             &= \int (\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})\rho \mathrm{d}\tau
\end{align}</math>
the force per unit volume is
<math display="block">\mathbf{f} = \rho\mathbf{E} + \mathbf{J} \times \mathbf{B}</math>
|2= Next, <math>\rho</math> and <math>\mathbf{J}</math> can be replaced by the fields <math>\mathbf{E}</math> and <math>\mathbf{B}</math>, using [[Gauss's law]] and [[Ampère's circuital law]]:
<math display="block">
  \mathbf{f} = \varepsilon_0\left(\boldsymbol{\nabla} \cdot \mathbf{E}\right)\mathbf{E} +
    \frac{1}{\mu_0}\left(\boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \mathbf{B}\right) \times \mathbf{B} -
    \varepsilon_0\frac{\partial\mathbf{E}}{\partial t} \times \mathbf{B}
</math>

|3= The time derivative can be rewritten to something that can be interpreted physically, namely the [[Poynting vector]]. Using the [[product rule]] and [[Faraday's law of induction]] gives
<math display="block">
  \frac{\partial}{\partial t} (\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}) =
  \frac{\partial\mathbf{E}}{\partial t} \times \mathbf{B} + \mathbf{E} \times \frac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t} =
    \frac{\partial\mathbf{E}}{\partial t} \times \mathbf{B} - \mathbf{E} \times (\boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \mathbf{E})
</math>
and we can now rewrite <math>\mathbf{f}</math> as
<math display="block">\mathbf{f} =
  \varepsilon_0\left(\boldsymbol{\nabla} \cdot \mathbf{E}\right)\mathbf{E} +
  \frac{1}{\mu_0}\left(\boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \mathbf{B}\right) \times \mathbf{B} -
  \varepsilon_0\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left(\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}\right) -
  \varepsilon_0\mathbf{E} \times (\boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \mathbf{E}),
</math>
then collecting terms with <math>\mathbf{E}</math> and <math>\mathbf{B}</math> gives
<math display="block">
  \mathbf{f} = \varepsilon_0\left[(\boldsymbol{\nabla} \cdot \mathbf{E}) \mathbf{E} - \mathbf{E} \times (\boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \mathbf{E})\right] +
    \frac{1}{\mu_0}\left[-\mathbf{B} \times \left(\boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \mathbf{B}\right)\right] -
    \varepsilon_0\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left(\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}\right).
</math>

|4= A term seems to be "missing" from the symmetry in <math>\mathbf{E}</math> and <math>\mathbf{B}</math>, which can be achieved by inserting <math>\left(\boldsymbol{\nabla} \cdot \mathbf{B}\right)\mathbf{B}</math> because of [[Gauss's law for magnetism]]:
<math display="block">
  \mathbf{f} = \varepsilon_0\left[(\boldsymbol{\nabla} \cdot \mathbf{E})\mathbf{E} - \mathbf{E} \times (\boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \mathbf{E})\right] +
    \frac{1}{\mu_0}\left[(\boldsymbol{\nabla} \cdot \mathbf{B})\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{B} \times \left(\boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \mathbf{B}\right)\right] -
    \varepsilon_0\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}\right).
</math>

Eliminating the curls (which are fairly complicated to calculate), using the [[vector calculus identity]]
<math display="block">
  \frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\nabla}(\mathbf{A} \cdot \mathbf{A}) =
    \mathbf{A} \times (\boldsymbol{\nabla} \times \mathbf{A}) + (\mathbf{A} \cdot \boldsymbol{\nabla})\mathbf{A},
</math>
leads to:
<math display="block">
  \mathbf{f} = \varepsilon_0\left[(\boldsymbol{\nabla} \cdot \mathbf{E})\mathbf{E} + (\mathbf{E} \cdot \boldsymbol{\nabla})\mathbf{E}\right] +
    \frac{1}{\mu_0}\left[(\boldsymbol{\nabla} \cdot \mathbf{B})\mathbf{B} + (\mathbf{B} \cdot \boldsymbol{\nabla})\mathbf{B}\right] -
    \frac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{\nabla}\left(\varepsilon_0 E^2 + \frac{1}{\mu_0} B^2\right) -
    \varepsilon_0\frac{\partial}{\partial t} \left(\mathbf{E} \times \mathbf{B}\right).
</math>

|5= This expression contains every aspect of electromagnetism and momentum and is relatively easy to compute. It can be written more compactly by introducing the '''Maxwell stress tensor''',
<math display="block">
  \sigma_{ij} \equiv \varepsilon_0\left(E_i E_j - \frac{1}{2} \delta_{ij}E^2\right) +
    \frac{1}{\mu_0} \left(B_i B_j - \frac{1}{2} \delta_{ij}B^2\right)
.</math>

All but the last term of <math>\mathbf{f}</math> can be written as the tensor [[divergence]] of the Maxwell stress tensor, giving:
<math display="block">\boldsymbol{\nabla} \cdot \boldsymbol{\sigma} = \mathbf{f} + \varepsilon_0 \mu_0 \frac{\partial\mathbf{S}}{\partial t}\,,</math>

As in the [[Poynting's theorem]], the second term on the right side of the above equation can be interpreted as the time derivative of the EM field's momentum density, while the first term is the time derivative of the momentum density for the massive particles. In this way, the above equation will be the law of conservation of momentum in classical electrodynamics; where the [[Poynting vector]],
<math display="block">\mathbf{S} = \frac{1}{\mu_0} \mathbf{E} \times\mathbf{B},</math>
has been introduced.

In the above relation for conservation of momentum, <math>\boldsymbol{\nabla} \cdot \boldsymbol{\sigma}</math> is the '''momentum flux density''' and plays a role similar to <math>\mathbf{S}</math> in [[Poynting's theorem]].

}}

== In magnetostatics ==
If the field is only magnetic (which is largely true in motors, for instance), some of the terms drop out, and the equation in SI units becomes:
<math display="block">\sigma_{ij} = \frac{1}{\mu_0} B_i B_j - \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0} \delta_{ij} \,.</math>

== In electrostatics ==

In [[electrostatics]] the effects of magnetism are not present. In this case the magnetic field vanishes, i.e. <math>\mathbf{B} = \mathbf{0}</math>, and we obtain the ''electrostatic Maxwell stress tensor''. It is given in component form by
<math display="block">
\sigma_{ij} = \varepsilon_0 E_i E_j - \frac{\varepsilon_0}{2} E^2\delta_{ij}
</math>
and in symbolic form by
<math display="block">
\boldsymbol{\sigma} = \varepsilon_0\mathbf{E} \otimes \mathbf{E} - \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 \left(\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{E}\right) \mathbf{I}
</math>
where <math>\mathbf{I}</math> is the appropriate identity tensor <math>\big(</math>usually <math>3\times3\big)</math>.

== Eigenvalue ==
The eigenvalues of the Maxwell stress tensor are given by:
<math display="block">\lambda = -\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2} E^2 - \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0} ,~ \pm\sqrt{\left(\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}E^2 - \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}\right)^2 + \frac{\varepsilon_0}{\mu_0} \left(\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{B}\right)^2}</math>

These eigenvalues are obtained by iteratively applying the [[matrix determinant lemma]], in conjunction with the [[Sherman–Morrison formula]].

Noting that the characteristic equation matrix, <math>\boldsymbol{\sigma} - \lambda\mathbf{\mathbb{I}}</math>, can be written as
<math display="block">\boldsymbol{\sigma} - \lambda\mathbf{\mathbb{I}} = -\left(\lambda + V\right)\mathbf{\mathbb{I}} + \varepsilon_0\mathbf{E}\mathbf{E}^\textsf{T} + \frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^\textsf{T}</math>
where
<math display="block">V = \frac{1}{2}\left(\varepsilon_0 E^2 + \frac{1}{\mu_0}B^2\right)</math>
we set
<math display="block">\mathbf{U} = -\left(\lambda + V\right)\mathbf{\mathbb{I}} + \varepsilon_0\mathbf{E}\mathbf{E}^\textsf{T}</math>

Applying the matrix determinant lemma once, this gives us
<math display="block">\det{\left(\boldsymbol{\sigma} - \lambda\mathbf{\mathbb{I}}\right)} = \left(1 + \frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf{B}^\textsf{T}\mathbf{U}^{-1}\mathbf{B}\right)\det{\left(\mathbf{U}\right)}</math>

Applying it again yields,
<math display="block">\det{\left(\boldsymbol{\sigma} - \lambda\mathbf{\mathbb{I}}\right)} = \left(1 + \frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf{B}^\textsf{T}\mathbf{U}^{-1}\mathbf{B}\right) \left(1 - \frac{\varepsilon_0\mathbf{E}^\textsf{T}\mathbf{E}}{\lambda + V}\right) \left(-\lambda - V\right)^3</math>

From the last multiplicand on the RHS, we immediately see that <math>\lambda = -V</math> is one of the eigenvalues.

To find the inverse of <math>\mathbf{U}</math>, we use the Sherman-Morrison formula:
<math display="block">\mathbf{U}^{-1} = -\left(\lambda + V\right)^{-1} - \frac{\varepsilon_0 \mathbf{E}\mathbf{E}^\textsf{T}}{\left(\lambda + V\right)^2 - \left(\lambda + V\right) \varepsilon_0\mathbf{E}^\textsf{T}\mathbf{E}}</math>

Factoring out a <math>\left(-\lambda - V \right)</math> term in the determinant, we are left with finding the zeros of the rational function:
<math display="block">\left[-\left(\lambda + V\right) - \frac{\varepsilon_0\left(\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{B}\right)^2}{\mu_0\left(-\left(\lambda + V\right) + \varepsilon_0\mathbf{E}^\textsf{T}\mathbf{E}\right)}\right] \left[-\left(\lambda + V\right) + \varepsilon_0\mathbf{E}^\textsf{T} \mathbf{E}\right]</math>

Thus, once we solve
<math display="block">-\left(\lambda + V\right) \left(-\left(\lambda + V\right) + \varepsilon_0 E^2\right) - \frac{\varepsilon_0}{\mu_0}\left(\mathbf{E} \cdot \mathbf{B}\right)^2 = 0</math>
we obtain the other two eigenvalues.
